{{Short description|Prime number with at least one million digits}}
A '''megaprime''' is a [[prime number]] with at least one million decimal digits.<ref>Chris Caldwell, [https://t5k.org/glossary/xpage/Megaprime.html The Prime Glossary: megaprime] at The [[PrimePages]]. Retrieved on 2008-01-04.</ref> 

Other terms for large primes include "titanic prime", coined by [[Samuel Yates]] in the 1980s for a prime with at least 1000 digits<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Prime Glossary: titanic prime |url=https://t5k.org/glossary/page.php?sort=TitanicPrime |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=t5k.org}}</ref> (of which the smallest is 10<sup>999</sup>+7),<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://factordb.com/index.php?id=1000000000022451023|title=factordb.com|website=factordb.com}}</ref> and "gigantic prime" for a prime with at least 10,000 digits<ref>Chris Caldwell, [https://t5k.org/glossary/xpage/GiganticPrime.html The Prime Glossary: gigantic prime] at The [[PrimePages]]. Retrieved on 2022-06-21.</ref> (of which the smallest is 10<sup>9999</sup>+33603).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://factordb.com/index.php?id=1100000000081719528|title=factordb.com|website=factordb.com}}</ref>

[[File:Megaprimes found by year.png|thumb|330px|Number of megaprimes found by year through 2025]]

{{As of|2026|1|1}}, there are 3,797 known megaprimes<ref name="The_largest_known_primes">Chris Caldwell, [https://t5k.org/primes/lists/all.txt The Largest Known Primes] at The PrimePages.</ref> which have more than 1,000,000 digits.<ref name="PRPTop">{{Cite web |title=Henri & Renaud Lifchitz's PRP Top records |url=http://www.primenumbers.net/prptop/prptop.php |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=www.primenumbers.net}}</ref> The first to be found was the [[Mersenne prime]] 2<sup>6972593</sup>−1 with 2,098,960 digits, discovered in 1999 by [[Nayan Hajratwala]], a participant in the [[distributed computing]] project [[GIMPS]].<ref name="1stmegaprime">{{Cite web |title=Mersenne Prime Discovery - 2^6972593-1 is Prime! |url=https://www.mersenne.org/primes/?press=M6972593 |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=www.mersenne.org}}</ref><ref name="largest">Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/notes/by_year.html ''The Largest Known Prime by Year: A Brief History''] at The PrimePages. Retrieved on 2008-09-28.</ref> Nayan was awarded a [[Cooperative Computing Award]] from the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]] for this achievement.

[[Almost all]] primes are megaprimes, as the number of primes with fewer than one million digits is finite. However, the vast majority of known primes are not megaprimes.

All numbers from 10<sup>999999</sup> through 10<sup>999999</sup> + 593498 are known to be [[composite number|composite]], and there is a very high probability that 10<sup>999999</sup> + 593499, a [[probable prime#Variants|strong probable prime]] for each of 8 different bases, is the smallest megaprime.<ref name="worldofnumbers">Patrick De Geest, [http://www.worldofnumbers.com/em_megaprp.htm 10^999999 + y], World!Of Numbers</ref> {{As of|2024}}, the smallest number known to be a megaprime is 10<sup>999999</sup> + 308267×10<sup>292000</sup> + 1.

The last prime that is not a megaprime is currently unknown. {{As of|2024}}, the largest prime number known to not be a megaprime is 10<sup>999999</sup> − 1022306×10<sup>287000</sup> − 1. There is a very high probability that 10<sup>999999</sup> &minus; 172473 is the biggest non-mega prime.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Henri & Renaud Lifchitz's PRP Top - Search by form |url=http://www.primenumbers.net/prptop/searchform.php?form=10%5E999999-a |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=www.primenumbers.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Border PRP's |url=https://www.worldofnumbers.com/borderprp.htm |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=www.worldofnumbers.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS |A340902 | Distance from the largest prime with less than 10^n decimal digits to 10^(10^n-1)}}</ref>
